claims.claim: A dietary pattern is the combination of foods and beverages that constitutes an individual's complete dietary intake over time; it represents the totality of what individuals habitually eat and drink.
The Dietary Guidelines state that an overall dietary pattern may better predict health status and disease risk than individual foods or nutrients.

MyPlate, the USDA food guidance icon launched in 2011 to replace the Food Guide Pyramid, organizes foods into five groups (fruits, vegetables, grains, protein foods, and dairy including fortified soy alternatives) with one-line messages such as 'make half your plate fruits and vegetables' and 'make half your grains whole grains.'

DASH (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension), a balanced eating plan developed with NHLBI support, emphasizes vegetables, fruits, whole grains, and low-fat or fat-free dairy while limiting saturated fat and sodium.
The Dietary Guidelines hold that a healthy eating pattern can be tailored to personal preferences, cultural traditions, and budgetary considerations.

Unhealthy diets are a major risk factor for disease and disability, while healthy diets help protect against malnutrition in all its forms and against noncommunicable diseases including diabetes, heart disease, stroke, and cancer.

The Dietary Guidelines for Americans are revised on a five-year cycle; the 2020-2025 edition carries the working definition used in this lesson, and the 10th edition (2025-2030) is the current one, hosted at RealFood.gov.
Healthy patterns are built on variety across and within food groups and on moderation in amounts and frequency, and the exact mixture is meant to fit a person's preferences, culture, and budget.

OpenStax's nutrition text notes the USDA's recognition that poor nutrition is a substantial factor in illness in the United States, linked to diabetes, obesity, and heart disease, and points to MyPlate and the Dietary Guidelines as evidence-based consumer guidance.
OpenStax's nutrition text frames nutrition as the study of how food and nutrients affect the body and health, providing the disciplinary context in which dietary guidance is developed and taught.

positions: The 2020-2025 edition (9th) carries the widely quoted working definition of a dietary pattern used in this lesson
The 10th edition (2025-2030), published at RealFood.gov, is the current guidance
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson attributes the working definition to the Dietary Guidelines and notes the edition; it treats the current edition as the continuation of the same guidance tradition and avoids edition-specific claims beyond the definition itself.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How prescriptive is a healthy pattern?
positions: The DGA hold that a healthy eating pattern can be adapted to personal preferences, cultural traditions, and budgetary considerations
Popular messaging often presents a single ideal diet as the only healthy pattern
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson follows the DGA framing: named patterns are examples, not fixed menus, and the mistakes section explicitly counters the one-diet-for-everyone idea.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The machine-generated draft contained only generic boilerplate ('Dietary Patterns is a foundational concept in Nutrition...') with no factual content; it was discarded in full and nothing from it was carried forward.
correctionsNeeded: Authored from scratch: the draft provided no working definition, food groups, or named patterns to correct; all content was written from the verified source set above.
